subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8! In this unit you will explore the world of geometric shapes, their properties, and the beautiful patterns of symmetry that appear all around you. From the hexagonal cells of a honeycomb, to the geometric tiling on the walls of a masjid in Mogadishu, to the round wheels of a lorry travelling from Hargeisa to Nairobi, shape and symmetry are everywhere. Your task this year is to learn to see them precisely and describe them with the correct mathematical language.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Understand that the number of sides of a regular polygon is equal to the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotation.
Identify and describe the hierarchy of quadrilaterals.
Understand and use Euler’s formula to connect number of vertices, faces and edges of 3D shapes.
Derive and use the fact that the exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
Understand π as the ratio between a circumference and a diameter. Know and use the formula for the circumference of a circle.
Construct triangles, midpoint and perpendicular bisector of a line segment, and the bisector of an angle.

outcomes: Identify lines of symmetry in shapes, letters and designs, and count them for regular polygons.
Describe rotational symmetry by its order and calculate the angle of rotation.
Classify triangles by their sides and angles, and quadrilaterals by their properties.
Explain the quadrilateral hierarchy and why a square is a special rectangle and a special rhombus.
Calculate interior and exterior angles of regular polygons.
Name the parts of a circle – radius, diameter, chord, tangent, arc, sector, segment – and use basic circle facts.
Count faces, edges and vertices of 3D solids and check answers with Euler's formula.

concepts.title: Lines of Symmetry (Reflection Symmetry)
concepts.explanation: A line of symmetry (also called a mirror line or line of reflection) is a line that divides a shape into two identical halves. If you fold the shape along this line, the two halves match exactly. You can also test with a small mirror: stand it on the line, and if the reflection completes the original shape, the line is a line of symmetry. Every point on one side has a matching point on the other side, the same distance from the line. The line acts like a mirror — one half is the exact reflection of the other.
concepts.example: Lines of symmetry in regular polygons

concepts.title: Rotational Symmetry
concepts.explanation:
A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks exactly the same after being turned by less than a full 360° about a central point, called the centre of rotation. The order of rotational symmetry is the number of times the shape looks identical during one complete turn.

The angle you turn through each time is easy to find: angle of rotation = 360° ÷ order. So a shape of order 4 matches itself every 360 ÷ 4 = 90°; a shape of order 3 matches every 120°; a shape of order 6 matches every 60°.

Order 1 means no rotational symmetry – the shape only looks the same after a full 360° turn. Every shape has at least order 1, so when a shape has no special rotational symmetry we say it has order 1.

Rotational symmetry in regular polygons

Just like lines of symmetry, regular polygons follow a clean rule: a regular polygon with n sides has rotational symmetry of order n.

Equilateral triangle: order 3 (matches at 120°, 240°, 360°).

Square: order 4 (matches at 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°).

Regular pentagon: order 5 (matches every 72°).

Regular hexagon: order 6 (matches every 60°).

Circle: infinite order – it matches at any angle at all.

Other shapes: a rectangle (that is not a square) has order 2 – it matches after a 180° turn. A rhombus and a parallelogram also have order 2. An isosceles or scalene triangle has order 1 (no rotational symmetry).

A special case worth naming is point symmetry: this is rotational symmetry of order 2, where the shape looks the same after a half turn (180°). The letter S, the letter N, the digit 8, and every parallelogram have point symmetry. Notice that the letter S has rotational symmetry of order 2 but no lines of symmetry at all – proof that the two kinds of symmetry are independent. A shape can have one without the other.
concepts.example: You can rotate a point using coordinates too, turning about the origin: a 90° anticlockwise turn sends (x, y) to (−y, x); a 180° turn sends (x, y) to (−x, −y); and a 270° anticlockwise turn sends (x, y) to (y, −x). These rules let you rotate a whole shape precisely, point by point.

concepts.title: Properties of Triangles
concepts.explanation:
A triangle is a polygon with three sides, three vertices and three angles. The three interior angles always add up to 180° – this is one of the most useful facts in all of geometry. We classify triangles in two ways: by their sides and by their angles.

Equilateral triangle: all three sides equal, all three angles equal to 60°. It has 3 lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 3.

Isosceles triangle: two sides equal and the two base angles equal. It has 1 line of symmetry and no rotational symmetry.

Scalene triangle: all three sides different and all three angles different. It has no symmetry at all.

Acute triangle: all three angles are less than 90°.

Right triangle: one angle is exactly 90°. The side opposite the right angle is the longest side, called the hypotenuse.

Obtuse triangle: one angle is greater than 90°.

These two systems overlap. A triangle can be, for example, a right isosceles triangle (angles 90°, 45°, 45°) or an acute scalene triangle. When Hassan builds a roof truss for a house in Garissa, he uses triangles precisely because a triangle is rigid – its shape cannot be pushed out of place the way a four-sided frame can. This is why triangles appear in bridges, cranes and pylons everywhere.
concepts.example: Because the angles of a triangle sum to 180°, you can always find a missing angle. If two angles of a triangle are 63° and 71°, the third must be 180 − 63 − 71 = 46°. In an isosceles triangle, once you know the apex angle you can find both equal base angles, since they must share what is left after subtracting from 180°.

concepts.title: Properties of Quadrilaterals
concepts.explanation: A quadrilateral is any four-sided polygon. Its four interior angles always add up to 360°. There are several important special quadrilaterals, and each is defined by its own properties. Learn them carefully. Parallelogram: 2 pairs of parallel sides; opposite sides and angles equal; diagonals bisect each other.
concepts.example: Parallelogram: order 2 rotational symmetry; 0 lines of symmetry.

concepts.title: The Quadrilateral Hierarchy
concepts.explanation: The special quadrilaterals form a family tree, or hierarchy, where some shapes are special cases of others. The key principle is this: a shape lower in the tree has all the properties of the shapes above it, plus extra properties of its own. Understanding this saves you from learning long lists by rote, because properties are inherited down the tree. Reading down the main branch: a quadrilateral becomes a parallelogram when it gains a second pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram becomes a rectangle when its angles become right angles (90°); it becomes a rhombus when its sides become equal; and it becomes a square when it has both right angles and equal sides.
concepts.example: This tree lets you judge statements about shapes. Some true statements: all squares are rectangles (a square meets every rectangle condition and adds more); all squares are rhombuses; all rectangles are parallelograms; all parallelograms are quadrilaterals. But the reverses are false: not all rectangles are squares, because a rectangle need not have equal sides; not all parallelograms are rectangles; not all quadrilaterals are parallelograms. The rule of thumb is that you can always travel up the tree (a square truly is a rectangle) but not always down it.

concepts.title: Polygons and Their Angles
concepts.explanation:
A polygon is a closed shape made of straight sides. A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal; an irregular polygon does not. For regular polygons there are two angle formulas you should know and be able to use.

⭐ Polygon Angle Formulas: each exterior angle of a regular n-sided polygon = 360 ÷ n. Each interior angle of a regular n-sided polygon = (n − 2) × 180 ÷ n. Interior angle + exterior angle = 180 (they lie on a straight line).

Why does the exterior angle rule work? If you walk all the way around the outside of any polygon, turning at each corner, you make one full turn of 360° by the time you return to the start. For a regular polygon, that 360° is shared equally among the n corners, so each exterior angle is 360 ÷ n. For a regular hexagon this gives 360 ÷ 6 = 60°, and so each interior angle is 180 − 60 = 120°.

The interior angle formula comes from splitting the polygon into triangles. Any polygon with n sides can be divided into (n − 2) triangles from a single vertex, and each triangle contributes 180°, so the interior angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°. Divide that total by n to get each angle in a regular polygon. Worked check: a regular pentagon has interior angle (5 − 2) × 180 ÷ 5 = 540 ÷ 5 = 108°; a regular octagon has (8 − 2) × 180 ÷ 8 = 1080 ÷ 8 = 135°.
concepts.example: These angles explain which regular shapes can tile a flat surface with no gaps. Squares (90°), equilateral triangles (60°) and regular hexagons (120°) all tile perfectly, because their angles divide exactly into 360°. That is precisely why bees build honeycomb from hexagons – it fills space with no waste and uses the least wax. You can see the same idea in the tiled geometric patterns of traditional architecture.

methods.title: How to find the order of rotational symmetry
methods.example: An equilateral triangle is turned about its centre. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
steps: Place a point at the centre of the shape.
Turn the shape slowly through one full 360° rotation.
Count how many times it looks exactly the same during the turn.
That count is the order. The angle of rotation is 360 ÷ order.

methods.title: How to find angles of a regular polygon
methods.example: Find the interior and exterior angles of a regular pentagon (5 sides).
steps: Count the number of sides, n.
Exterior angle = 360 ÷ n.
Interior angle = 180 − exterior angle (or use (n − 2) × 180 ÷ n).
Check: interior + exterior should equal 180.

methods.title: How to count faces, edges and vertices
methods.example: A square-based pyramid has how many faces, edges and vertices? Verify using Euler’s formula.
steps: Faces: count every flat surface.
Edges: count every line where two faces meet.
Vertices: count every corner point.
Check with Euler's formula: V − E + F should equal 2 for a polyhedron.

methods.title: Naming a quadrilateral from clues
methods.example: A quadrilateral has four equal sides but its angles are not right angles. What is it?
steps: Four equal sides is the defining property of a rhombus.
Because the angles are not right angles, it is not a square.
So the shape is a rhombus.
(If the angles were right angles too, it would be a square.)

methods.title: Interior angle of a regular polygon
methods.example: Find each interior angle of a regular decagon (10 sides).
steps: Check: each exterior angle = 360 ÷ 10 = 36°, and 144 + 36 = 180.
Correct.

methods.title: Faces, edges and vertices with Euler
methods.example: A pentagonal prism has how many faces, edges and vertices? Verify with Euler's formula.
steps: For a prism with an s-sided base: faces = s + 2 = 5 + 2 = 7; edges = 3s = 3 × 5 = 15; vertices = 2s = 2 × 5 = 10.
Euler check: V − E + F = 10 − 15 + 7 = 2.
Correct.

workedExamples.title: Lines of symmetry of a regular polygon
workedExamples.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a regular octagon have?
workedExamples.solution: A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry. An octagon has 8 sides, so it has 8 lines of symmetry. (It also has rotational symmetry of order 8.)

workedExamples.title: Order and angle of rotational symmetry
workedExamples.prompt: A shape has rotational symmetry of order 5. What is its angle of rotation?
workedExamples.solution: Angle of rotation = 360 ÷ order = 360 ÷ 5 = 72°. The shape matches itself every 72° as it turns.

workedExamples.title: Missing angle in a triangle
workedExamples.prompt: Two angles of a triangle are 58° and 74°. Find the third angle, and classify the triangle by its angles.
workedExamples.solution: The angles of a triangle sum to 180°. Third angle = 180 − 58 − 74 = 48°. All three angles (58°, 74°, 48°) are less than 90°, so it is an acute triangle. Since all three are different, it is also scalene.

workedExamples.title: Naming a quadrilateral from clues
workedExamples.prompt: A quadrilateral has four equal sides but its angles are not right angles. What is it?
workedExamples.solution: Four equal sides is the defining property of a rhombus. Because the angles are not right angles, it is not a square. So the shape is a rhombus. (If the angles were right angles too, it would be a square.)

workedExamples.title: Interior angle of a regular polygon
workedExamples.prompt: Find each interior angle of a regular decagon (10 sides).
workedExamples.solution: Each interior angle = (n − 2) × 180 ÷ n = (10 − 2) × 180 ÷ 10 = 8 × 180 ÷ 10 = 1440 ÷ 10 = 144°. Check: each exterior angle = 360 ÷ 10 = 36°, and 144 + 36 = 180. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Faces, edges and vertices with Euler
workedExamples.prompt: A pentagonal prism has how many faces, edges and vertices? Verify with Euler's formula.
workedExamples.solution: For a prism with an s-sided base: faces = s + 2 = 5 + 2 = 7; edges = 3s = 3 × 5 = 15; vertices = 2s = 2 × 5 = 10. Euler check: V − E + F = 10 − 15 + 7 = 2. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Circle vocabulary and diameter
workedExamples.prompt: A circle has a radius of 7 cm. What is its diameter, and what is the name of the longest possible chord?
workedExamples.solution: Diameter = 2 × radius = 2 × 7 = 14 cm. The longest chord in any circle is the diameter itself, because it passes through the centre.

workedExamples.title: Identifying a transformation
workedExamples.prompt: Shape A is mapped onto shape B, which is the same size but flipped so that left and right are swapped. What single transformation is this, and are A and B congruent?
workedExamples.solution: A flip that swaps left and right and reverses orientation is a reflection in a vertical mirror line. Because a reflection keeps the size and shape unchanged, A and B are congruent.

workedExamples.title: Faces, edges and vertices of a hexagonal prism
workedExamples.prompt: For a hexagonal prism, work out the faces, edges and vertices, then verify with Euler's formula.
workedExamples.solution: For a prism with an s-sided base: faces = s + 2 = 6 + 2 = 8; edges = 3s = 3 × 6 = 18; vertices = 2s = 2 × 6 = 12. Euler check: V − E + F = 12 − 18 + 8 = 2. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Symmetry of a rhombus
workedExamples.prompt: Copy and complete: a rhombus has ___ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order ___.
workedExamples.solution: A rhombus has 2 lines of symmetry (along its diagonals) and rotational symmetry of order 2.

workedExamples.title: Reflecting a point in the coordinate axes
workedExamples.prompt: Reflect the point (3, 5) in a) the y-axis b) the x-axis. Give the new coordinates.
workedExamples.solution: Reflecting in the y-axis keeps y the same and reverses the sign of x: (3, 5) → (−3, 5). Reflecting in the x-axis keeps x the same and reverses the sign of y: (3, 5) → (3, −5).

workedExamples.title: True or false: parallelograms and squares
workedExamples.prompt: True or false, with a reason: a) all parallelograms are rectangles b) all squares are parallelograms.
workedExamples.solution: a) False — a parallelogram does not need right angles (for example, a non-rectangular rhombus is a parallelogram), so it is not always a rectangle. b) True — a square has two pairs of parallel sides, so it satisfies the definition of a parallelogram.

activities.title: Fold-and-Cut Symmetry Designs
steps: Fold a sheet of paper once down the middle. The fold is your line of symmetry.
Cut a design into the folded edge, then open the paper to reveal a symmetrical shape.
Now fold a fresh sheet twice (in half, then in half again) and cut. How many lines of symmetry does the result have?
Challenge: fold to make a design with rotational symmetry, like a paper snowflake, and count its order.
Keep your best designs and label each with its number of lines of symmetry and its order of rotational symmetry.

activities.title: Build a Solid from a Net
activities.materials: card or stiff paper, a ruler, a pencil, scissors, glue or tape.
steps: Draw the net of a cube: a cross of 6 equal squares (four in a row, one above and one below the second square).
Cut it out, fold along every line, and glue the edges to form the cube.
Count the faces, edges and vertices of your finished cube. Check with Euler's formula: V − E + F should equal 2.
Now design and build a triangular prism or a square pyramid the same way.

activities.title: The Quadrilateral Detective Game
steps: On separate cards write clues such as 'four equal sides', 'four right angles', 'one pair of parallel sides', 'diagonals perpendicular'.

A player draws two or three clue cards and must name a quadrilateral that fits all of them. If you are working alone, shuffle the cards face down, draw them yourself, and check your reasoning with your AI tutor.
Discuss: is there more than one possible answer? Which clues force a single shape?
Take turns being the detective if you have a partner, or keep drawing fresh cards for yourself. Use the family tree to check every answer.
This game trains you to reason from properties to shapes – exactly what geometry proof requires.

activities.title: Symmetry Hunt (Investigation)
steps: Walk around your home, street or masjid and find ten objects or patterns with symmetry.
For each one, record whether it has line symmetry, rotational symmetry, or both.
Sketch three of the most interesting patterns and mark their lines of symmetry.
Which was more common in what you found – line symmetry or rotational symmetry? Write down what you notice.

activities.title: Angle Explorer with Regular Polygons
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, a protractor if you have one.
steps: Draw a regular triangle, square, pentagon and hexagon as neatly as you can.
For each, calculate the exterior angle (360 ÷ n) and the interior angle (180 − exterior).
Check which of your shapes could tile a floor with no gaps, and explain why using the interior angle.
Design a small tiling pattern using one of the shapes that works.

activities.title: Family Tiling Design (Group Task)
activities.materials: your family or friends if available (or work solo), coloured paper, scissors.
steps: Together with family or friends – or on your own if working solo – cut many identical regular hexagons (or squares, or triangles).
Arrange them to cover a sheet with no gaps and no overlaps – a tessellation.
Add colour to bring out lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry in the finished pattern.
Talk about where you have seen such patterns before – on rugs, walls, or tiled floors.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand symmetry or 3D solids best? What was the trickiest part? Did building a net change how you see boxes and packaging around you? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Lines of Symmetry in a Regular Polygon
rules.text: The general rule: a regular polygon with n sides has exactly n lines of symmetry. So a regular octagon (8 sides) has 8 lines of symmetry, and a regular decagon (10 sides) has 10. A circle is the extreme case – any line through its centre is a line of symmetry, so it has infinitely many.

rules.title: Rotational Symmetry in a Regular Polygon
rules.text: Just like lines of symmetry, regular polygons follow a clean rule: a regular polygon with n sides has rotational symmetry of order n.

rules.title: Reasoning with the Quadrilateral Hierarchy
rules.text: This tree lets you judge statements about shapes. Some true statements: all squares are rectangles (a square meets every rectangle condition and adds more); all squares are rhombuses; all rectangles are parallelograms; all parallelograms are quadrilaterals. But the reverses are false: not all rectangles are squares, because a rectangle need not have equal sides; not all parallelograms are rectangles; not all quadrilaterals are parallelograms. The rule of thumb is that you can always travel up the tree (a square truly is a rectangle) but not always down it.

rules.title: Why the Exterior Angle Rule Works
rules.text: Why does the exterior angle rule work? If you walk all the way around the outside of any polygon, turning at each corner, you make one full turn of 360° by the time you return to the start. For a regular polygon, that 360° is shared equally among the n corners, so each exterior angle is 360 ÷ n. For a regular hexagon this gives 360 ÷ 6 = 60°, and so each interior angle is 180 − 60 = 120°.

realProblems.prompt: Ibrahim is cutting a geometric star pattern for a decoration. He wants a design with rotational symmetry of order 6 but NO lines of symmetry. Is this possible? Describe how such a design could look.
realProblems.answer: Yes — a design like a six-bladed fan or pinwheel with all blades curved the same way has rotational symmetry of order 6 but no mirror line, because reflecting it reverses the 'spin'.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the question is really about (Line of symmetry, Order of rotational symmetry, Regular polygon), then work one step at a time and check the answer is sensible.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Yes — a design like a six-bladed fan or pinwheel with all blades curved the same way has rotational symmetry of order 6 but no mirror line, because reflecting it reverses the 'spin'.

realProblems.prompt: A water tank in Kismaayo is a cylinder. Describe its faces, edges and vertices. Then explain why Euler's formula does not apply to it.
realProblems.answer: A cylinder has 2 circular faces, 1 curved surface, 2 circular edges and 0 vertices; Euler's formula applies only to polyhedra (flat faces, straight edges), and a cylinder has a curved surface, so the formula does not apply.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the question is really about (Line of symmetry, Order of rotational symmetry, Regular polygon), then work one step at a time and check the answer is sensible.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A cylinder has 2 circular faces, 1 curved surface, 2 circular edges and 0 vertices; Euler's formula applies only to polyhedra (flat faces, straight edges), and a cylinder has a curved surface, so the formula does not apply.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A regular polygon has an exterior angle of 24°. How many sides does it have, and what is each interior angle?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Number of sides = 360 ÷ 24 = 15 sides; each interior angle = 180 − 24 = 156°.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides and one line of symmetry. Name it.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: An isosceles trapezium (one pair of parallel sides, one line of symmetry).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A polyhedron has 12 edges and 6 faces. Use Euler's formula to find the number of vertices, and name a solid it could be.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: V − E + F = 2, so V − 12 + 6 = 2, giving V = 8; a solid with 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces is a cube (or cuboid).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A parallelogram has perpendicular diagonals but its angles are not right angles. What special quadrilateral is it? Justify your answer using the hierarchy.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Perpendicular diagonals is the special property of a rhombus; since the angles are not right angles it is not a square, so it must be a rhombus.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain, using interior angles, why regular pentagons cannot tile a flat surface on their own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A regular pentagon has interior angle 108°; 360 ÷ 108 is not a whole number (it is about 3.33), so pentagons cannot meet around a point without gaps or overlaps.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Polygons and Their Angles.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A polygon is a closed shape made of straight sides. A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal; an irregular polygon does not. For regular polygons there are two angle formulas you should know and be able to use. ⭐ Polygon Angle Formulas: each exterior angle of a regular n-sided polygon = 360 ÷ n. Each interior angle of a regular n-sided polygon = (n − 2) × 180 ÷ n. Interior angle + exterior angle = 180 (they lie on a straight line).

selfAssessment: I can identify lines of symmetry in shapes, letters and designs, and count them for regular polygons.
I can describe rotational symmetry by its order and calculate the angle of rotation.
I can classify triangles by their sides and angles, and quadrilaterals by their properties.
I can explain the quadrilateral hierarchy and why a square is a special rectangle and a special rhombus.
I can calculate interior and exterior angles of regular polygons.
I can name the parts of a circle – radius, diameter, chord, tangent, arc, sector, segment – and use basic circle facts.
I can count faces, edges and vertices of 3D solids and check answers with Euler's formula.
